Q: How does a skill differ from a tool?
explain: A tool is an executable capability. A skill explains a reusable way to perform work, potentially using several tools and resources. A host instruction defines overarching behavior. Keep these layers distinct so procedural text does not accidentally grant authority.
example: A review skill says how to assess citations; the read-source tool still decides which sources the caller may access.
takeaway: Expertise instructions and execution permissions are different things.

explain: Short metadata helps choose a relevant method without filling the prompt with every manual. Load the procedure after selection and supporting material only when required. Evaluate whether the metadata actually chooses the right skill.
example: An answer-review task loads a support rubric, not the spreadsheet-export procedure and its dependencies.
takeaway: Selective loading preserves useful context space.

Q: What makes a skill package maintainable?
explain: Give it a clear trigger, expected inputs, outputs, steps, dependencies, and failure behavior. Version scripts and referenced tool contracts. Use synthetic examples and keep credentials outside the package.
example: A tool schema change triggers a skill compatibility test rather than silently breaking its instructions.
takeaway: A skill is an interface with dependencies, not a loose prompt file.

Q: How should conflicting instructions be handled?
explain: Follow the host's actual precedence and execution policy. Stable security constraints should not be duplicated inconsistently inside task packages. Treat external skill content and scripts as inputs requiring review.
example: A skill requests all customer files while the current task permits one case. The runtime denies the excess scope.
takeaway: Capability checks remain authoritative when instructions disagree.

Q: What makes a skill discoverable and teachable?
explain: Describe the task it solves, when to use it, necessary inputs, expected outputs, and when another mechanism is appropriate. Keep the entry instructions short and move detail into referenced resources. Include one normal case, one boundary case, and a clear failure path. Version the package so behavior changes can be traced.
example: A citation-audit skill describes checking claim support and retrieving bounded spans. It does not trigger merely because a document mentions citations in passing.
takeaway: Narrow purpose and concrete examples improve selection and use.

Q: How should a skill call a script without creating an injection path?
explain: Use a structured argument interface, validate identifiers and paths, and avoid constructing shell commands from untrusted text. Restrict filesystem and network access independently of the instructions. Review dependencies and record which inputs and artifacts the helper touches. Skill text is not a substitute for process permissions.
example: A document title containing shell metacharacters remains a string argument, never executable command text. A file helper rejects paths outside its permitted working area.
takeaway: Helper execution needs ordinary secure software boundaries.
